paper_metadata.title: A Survey on Generative Knowledge Graph Construction
paper_metadata.abstract: This survey reviews generative knowledge graph construction, contrasting conventional sequence-to-sequence approaches with LLM-driven construction. It covers LLM roles in ontology construction, knowledge extraction, and knowledge fusion, compares advantages and limitations, and identifies future work on architecture optimization, multimodal integration, and intelligent fusion.

problem_addressed: The paper addresses how generative methods can automate knowledge graph construction from unstructured or semi-structured sources and overcome limitations of discriminative pipeline approaches, especially error propagation and limited cross-domain generalization. Its objective is to survey the evolution from Seq2Seq generation to LLM-driven full-process construction and compare their mechanisms, applications, benefits, limitations, and future directions.

methodology.description: This is a narrative survey, not a newly evaluated KGC model. It frames KGC as mapping raw data and background knowledge to a graph, then classifies the literature into discriminative and generative paradigms. For generative extraction, input text x is mapped autoregressively to a linearized target sequence y of triples/structures; pretrained Seq2Seq models such as MASS, T5, and BART can be fine-tuned with cross-entropy. It reviews: (1) copy-based generation, where a decoder copies subject/object spans from input while selecting relation labels, with reinforcement learning for triple order and Top-k pruning for documents; (2) structure-linearization, which serializes events/triples and can constrain decoding with event schemas; and (3) label-augmented generation, which inserts explicit entity/type labels in natural-language-like output. For LLM-era KGC, the surveyed execution patterns include top-down ontology assistance (natural-language requirements to formal ontology), bottom-up schema induction (open extraction, clustering, definition, and canonicalization), schema-guided or schema-free extraction, and schema-/instance-level fusion through alignment, disambiguation, conflict resolution, and verification. Review-level inference: because this paper synthesizes methods rather than implementing one, descriptions of architecture, prompts, training, and pipelines are literature-level categories, not a single reproducible workflow authored and tested by Zhao and Huang.

ontology_or_schema_use.value: The survey treats background knowledge, rules, schemas, type hierarchies, and domain ontologies as constraints on the semantic space of a KG. It reviews top-down LLM-assisted ontology modelling from natural-language requirements into formal ontology; bottom-up schema induction through open extraction and clustering; ontology-guided RDF triple extraction; dynamic/evolving schemas; and schema-level alignment/canonicalization during fusion. Schema use is therefore a major reviewed component, not an ontology implemented by this survey.

input_output.input_type: The surveyed KGC problem uses unstructured or semi-structured data sources, especially natural-language text/sentences/documents; the general formulation also permits webpages, tables, and multimodal content.
input_output.input_granularity: The reviewed methods operate at sentence level for relational facts, with extensions to document-level extraction, cross-sentence event detection, and large-scale corpora for schema induction.
input_output.output_representation: The reviewed outputs include entities, entity categories/types, relation facts and triples, event structures, linked entities, RDF triples, formal ontologies/schemas, and constructed or fused knowledge graphs. Generative systems commonly linearize triples or event structures into text sequences before decoding them into structured graph content.

evaluation.setting: No original empirical benchmark, dataset, metric, baseline, or quantitative experiment is presented. The paper is a qualitative survey that compares families of generative KGC approaches through narrative discussion and Table 1.

value: The survey concludes that conventional Seq2Seq generation provides end-to-end knowledge extraction and can reduce error accumulation associated with discriminative pipelines.

It classifies traditional generative approaches into copy-based, structure-linearization-based, and label-enhanced sequence generation, and LLM-era work into ontology construction, knowledge extraction, and knowledge fusion.

Its qualitative comparison finds that copy-based generation reduces entity hallucination/repetition and works well for overlapping relations; structural linearization offers uniform output and high semantic consistency; label enhancement improves type/relation distinction and is stable in low-resource and cross-task settings; LLM methods offer adaptation, ontology evolution, extraction, and semantic fusion but face controllability, evaluation, computational, and scalability issues.
It identifies architecture/explainability, unified and multimodal construction, and intelligent/dynamic fusion for cognitive applications as future research directions.

value: Author synthesis: copy-based sequence generation explicitly copies entities, reducing entity hallucination and repeated generation; it is strong for overlapping-relation extraction.
Author synthesis: structure-linearization methods provide a uniform output format, high semantic consistency, and can extend to event extraction and entity linking.
Author synthesis: label-enhanced generation exposes label semantics, improves distinction of entity/relation types, and is reported as stable in low-resource and cross-task settings.

Author synthesis: LLM-assisted ontology construction supports semantic consistency, automation, and schema co-evolution; LLM extraction can generate triples without a manually supplied ontology and adapt across domains; LLM fusion combines multi-source information with semantic consistency and end-to-end integration/verification.

Review-level inference: the survey's taxonomy connects pre-LLM Seq2Seq mechanisms with LLM-era ontology, extraction, and fusion workflows, making it useful for methodology-level comparison rather than single-model performance selection.

value: Author synthesis: copy-based methods are sensitive to long text and complex sentence structures, and relation generation still depends on a closed label set.
Author synthesis: structure-linearization has a large decoding space and high inference cost; label errors and structural drift become more pronounced for long text.
Author synthesis: label-enhanced methods produce long outputs, can omit or misplace labels, are sensitive to label design, and need additional template optimization to generalize to open domains.

Author synthesis: LLM ontology construction lacks systematic evaluation and standardized output; LLM extraction has weak consistency/controllability and may drift semantically; LLM fusion requires substantial compute and human verification and has an efficiency bottleneck at scale.

Review-level inference: since no systematic search protocol, study-selection procedure, dataset comparison, or quantitative synthesis is reported in the paper, its comparative claims should be used as qualitative orientation rather than as a measured ranking of methods.
